This project is an exploration of linear models. Models are estimated by linear regression.  The data set is from Motor Trend magazine.

The assignment is based on estimation of 3 models:
1. mpg as a function of wt
2. mpg as a function of disp
3  mpg as a function of both wt and disp

Complete a linear model with data description, a model fit a, and a prediction of mpg based on weigth of 3.050 lbs, with a displacement of 122 cubic inches (this is 2.5 L).

use an anova to compare model 2 with model 3

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```
# Load the dataset (built-in)

```{r}
data(mtcars)
```

# View first 6 rows and summary
```{r}
head(mtcars)
```

# Model 1:
 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt (wt) is the predictor (X)

## data summary
### graphical summary

```{r}
plot(mpg~wt,data=mtcars,   pch=15)
grid()
```

The scatterplot shows a correlation between higher wt and lower mpg.

### numerical summary
```{r}
cor(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
```


### model summary

```{r}
model1 <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
summary(model1)
```
The equation we found is y=37.28-5.34*wt.
```{r}
newData = data.frame(wt=3.050, disp=122)
print(predict(model1, newData, interval = 'predict'))
```
### predicted mpg
The predicted mpg is 21, when rounded up. The confidence interval will be between 15 and 27.


# Model 3 :

 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt and disp are the predictors (X's)

## data summary
### graphical summary
```{r}
plot(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars,    pch=15)
grid()
```


The two scatterplots display similar correlations between lower mpg and higher wt and disp.

### numerical summary
There is no numerical summary for Model 3.

### model summary
model3= lm(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)
model summary (coefficients, R², etc.), summarize the fit

```{r}
model3= lm(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)
summary(model3)
```
 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt (wt) and displacement (disp) are the predictors (X's)

### model summary
```{r}
model3 <- lm(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)
summary(model3)
```

```{r}
newData = data.frame(wt=3.050, disp=122)
print(predict(model1, newData, interval = 'predict'))
```

# anova: compare models 2 and 3

model3 <- lm(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)

model summary (coefficients, R², etc.)

### predicted mpg
```{r}
print(predict(model1, newData, interval = 'predict'))
```


```{r}
anova_result <- anova(model1, model3)
print(anova_result)
```
The F value is greater than .05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis if there was one.
Adding the additional variable of displacement did not make it better.

# Discussion and Conculsions

Did displacement add any information to the model? No it did not.
The model with displacement added to weight was functionally the same as a model with just weight.
